system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2132-09-23 00:25:00 to 2132-09-26 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with a history of HCV and alcoholic cirrhosis, portal hypertension, esophageal varices, and depression presented with acute right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and subjective fever. She had elevated liver enzymes, lactate, and transaminases with AST greater than ALT, concerning for mild alcoholic hepatitis and possible colitis. CT abdomen showed circumferential cecal wall thickening likely due to portal colopathy. Empiric antibiotics were started. Endoscopy revealed stable small esophageal varices and severe portal hypertensive gastropathy; a benign-appearing 5 mm polyp in the descending colon was removed. Her symptoms improved with supportive care, fluid resuscitation, and treatment of alcohol withdrawal. She was discharged home with improved pain, stable labs, and instructions to follow up on polyp biopsy, repeat EGD in one year, and hepatitis B vaccination.

Internal hemorrhoids without mention of complication

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  MRCP

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman s/p cholecystecomy, h/o EtOH cirrhosis, p/w RUQ
pain and chills c/f cholangitis  // choledocholithiasis?

TECHNIQUE:  T1 and T2 weighted multiplanar images of the abdomen were acquired
within a 1.5 T magnet, including 3D dynamic sequences obtained prior to,
during, and following the administration of 7 cc of Gadavist intravenous
contrast.  The patient also received oral contrast of 1 cc of Gadavist diluted
in 50 cc of water.

COMPARISON:  CT ___, CT ___, Ultrasound ___

FINDINGS: 

MRCP WITH AND WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:  The study is limited by respiratory
motion. The liver is shrunken and nodular in keeping with known cirrhosis.
There is no significant loss of signal on the out of phase images relative to
the in phase images to suggest hepatic steatosis. A 2.6 x 2.3 cm mass in
segment II demonstrates mild T2 hypointensity, restricted diffusion, arterial
hyperenhancement, and washout on the delayed phase (5:18, 8:27,1401:54,
1403:54), meeting criteria for HCC, OPTN 5B.  Sub-centimeter peripheral
arterially-enhancing foci in segment II (1401:49) and segment V (1401:84)
without correlates on the other sequences are likely transient hepatic
intensity differences.

Dilation of the common duct to 8 mm is unchanged from ultrasound ___ when it was 10 mm and CT ___, with smooth distal tapering. No
filling defect is seen within the common bile duct to suggest a stone. No
filling defect is seen in the cystic duct remnant. There is no intrahepatic
bile duct dilation.  Post contrast imaging is limited by respiratory motion,
but there is no ___ enhancement.  No intrahepatic fluid collection
identified.

The spleen is not enlarged, measuring 12.1 cm. No focal splenic lesion is
identified.

The pancreas is normal in signal intensity without focal lesion identified.
The main pancreatic duct is not dilated.

Bilateral adrenal glands are normal. The kidneys enhance symmetrically without
hydronephrosis. Multiple nonenhancing T2 hyperintense lesions in both kidneys
are simple cysts. The visualized bowel is grossly unremarkable. There is no
ascites in the upper abdomen. A 10 mm porta hepatic lymph node is likely
related to liver disease (8: 28).

The abdominal aorta is normal in caliber. The main portal vein, splenic vein
and SMV are patent. The paraumbilical vein is recanalized with caput medusae.

No concerning osseous abnormality is identified.

IMPRESSION: 

1. 2.6 cm mass in hepatic segment II meets OPTN-5B criteria for HCC.
2. CBD dilation is unchanged from ___, within cholecystectomy
limits. No choledocholithiasis. No intrahepatic bile duct dilation or MR
evidence for active cholangitis.
3. Cirrhosis with evidence of portal hypertension including recanalized
paraumbilical vein and caput medusae. No splenomegaly or ascites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having right-sided abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about two days ago. It’s sharp and constant in the upper right side. I’ve been nauseous and threw up a few times—some was brownish, but no red blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, jaundice, or dark urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No yellow skin or eyes. I did feel a bit warm, but no confirmed fever. Urine seems normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You have a history of cirrhosis from hepatitis C and alcohol. When was your last drink?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a small sip about two weeks ago. I’ve been trying to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Your vitals are stable, and your labs show low white blood cells but no signs of infection so far. We’re concerned the pain might be from your bile duct.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bile duct? Like gallstones? But I had my gallbladder out years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But the common bile duct can still get blocked or dilated. Your CT scan shows it’s wider than before—11 mm, up from 6 mm. We’re not seeing a stone, but it could be sphincter of Oddi dysfunction or something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted hepatology. They recommend antibiotics just in case and an MRCP tomorrow morning—it’s a special MRI that looks closely at the bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will that tell us what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help. We’re also watching your liver enzymes. They’re elevated, especially AST, which can happen with alcohol or other stress on the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m back to update you. Your MRCP is scheduled for today. Any change in pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurting, but I haven’t vomited since last night. I’m tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving you fluids and Zofran for nausea. The MRCP will give us clearer answers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I have the MRCP results. There’s no stone in the bile duct, so that’s good. But we found something else—a 2.6 cm mass in your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A mass? Is it cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It meets the imaging criteria for hepatocellular carcinoma—liver cancer. Given your cirrhosis, this is a known risk. We’ll discuss treatment options at a tumor board meeting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh my god. Is it serious? Can it be treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but because it’s small and localized, the outlook is better. Likely treatment is radiofrequency ablation—using heat to destroy the tumor. Your gastroenterologist will guide you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared. My mom died from liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry. We’ll support you through this. The most important thing now is to stay off alcohol completely—it protects your liver and improves treatment success.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show something new—your CK, a muscle enzyme, is very high. And AST is now 868.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: CK? I’ve heard that before. Isn’t that from muscle breakdown?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—rhabdomyolysis. It can happen with seizures, especially alcohol withdrawal. You denied drinking, but your past records show similar spikes after unreported drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t have a seizure. I don’t remember anything like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may have happened before you came in. We’re giving IV fluids to protect your kidneys. Your kidney function is stable so far, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will this go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with hydration. But we’ll refer you to rheumatology. You have a history of anti-smooth muscle antibodies, so we want to rule out autoimmune causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative—no infection. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the cancer meeting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow. They’ll decide the best approach. You’ll follow up with your GI doctor afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tumor board reviewed your case. They recommend radiofrequency ablation. It’s minimally invasive and done as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your GI doctor will schedule it. In the meantime, your pain is improving, and we’re stopping IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve been anxious this whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ve continued your sertraline and Seroquel. Talk to your psychiatrist about adjusting them if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. Your vitals are stable, and labs are trending better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your medications—especially lactulose, rifaximin, and your vitamins. Use tramadol only as needed for pain, and don’t drive or drink alcohol with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your gastroenterologist soon to discuss the ablation. Also schedule visits with rheumatology and your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the muscle issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rheumatology will check for autoimmune causes. But staying hydrated and avoiding alcohol will help prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge summary explains everything, and your medications are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s a lot to process, but I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Take it one step at a time. Call your doctor if pain worsens or you feel confused, weak, or short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’m really stopping drinking this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do for your liver and your treatment. We’re here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Someone will bring your discharge papers. A nurse will walk you out when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up on everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Stay strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on your side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call if I need anything.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with a history of alcoholic and HCV-related cirrhosis was admitted for severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Initial imaging showed dilation of the common bile duct, prompting an MRCP, which revealed a 2.6 cm liver mass meeting criteria for hepatocellular carcinoma. The diagnosis was discussed with the patient and family, and treatment planning was initiated through a tumor board, with likely radiofrequency ablation recommended. During the hospitalization, she developed markedly elevated CK and AST, consistent with rhabdomyolysis, possibly due to an unwitnessed alcohol withdrawal seizure, though no active withdrawal was observed. She remained stable, pain improved with supportive care, and she was discharged home with follow-up plans for oncology, gastroenterology, and rheumatology. Alcohol cessation was strongly emphasized.
